summary: Defines additional CBOR tags for time, duration, and period. RFC 8949 only defines tags 0 (RFC 3339 string time) and 1 (POSIX time). Newer requirements called for further ways to express time in CBOR, and this document provides them.

eli5.summary: Computers need to write down dates and lengths of time in small packages. This adds new ways to do so in a compact data format.

questions: cbor tags for time and duration
how to encode nanoseconds in cbor
subtitle: Three new CBOR tags for richer timestamps, durations and time periods.

tldr.problem: CBOR tags 0 and 1 only cover RFC 3339 strings and POSIX time as an integer or float, which limits resolution to roughly microseconds and assumes UTC. Newer uses needed finer resolution, other timescales and extra context.
tldr.mechanism: Tag 1001 wraps a map with one base time plus optional keys for sub-second fractions, timescale, clock quality, time zone hints and IXDTF suffixes. Tag 1002 reuses the same map for durations, and tag 1003 builds periods from times and durations.
tldr.outcome: IANA allocated tags 1001, 1002 and 1003 and created two new registries, Timescales and Time Tag Map Keys, so more keys and timescales can be added later.

today: RFC 9581 is a Proposed Standard and, per the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It is the reference for CBOR tags 1001, 1002 and 1003.

sections.title: Why More Time Tags
sections.content:
CBOR (RFC 8949) is a compact data format that can be extended with tags registered at IANA. RFC 8949 defines two time tags: tag 0 for an RFC 3339 time string and tag 1 for POSIX time as an int or float.

This RFC lists what those two cannot do. Tag 1 holds at most a binary64 floating-point value, which limits resolution to approximately microseconds at the time of writing. Tags 0 and 1 are defined for UTC, though some interchanges are better done on TAI. And there is no standard way to carry intent about interpretation, such as time zone or calendar, for times that lie in the future.

The RFC defines one new time tag and two related tags, for durations and periods, and is the reference document for their IANA registration.
sections.eli5: The old time tags could not write down very tiny slices of a second or say which clock was used. These new ones can.

sections.title: The Extended Time Map (Tag 1001)
sections.content:
An extended time is CBOR tag 1001 wrapped around a map. The map MUST contain exactly one unsigned integer key that gives the base time. It MAY also contain negative integer or text string keys with supplementary information, and unsigned integer keys explicitly defined as critical.

The key's sign tells a reader how to treat unknown keys. Negative integer and text string keys are elective: implementations MUST ignore pairs they do not understand, since the time is still usable without them. Unsigned integer keys are base time or critical, so implementations MUST signal an error on ones they do not understand.

Key 1 is a base time exactly like a tag 1 value, and keys 4 and 5 hold a decimal fraction or bigfloat array as for CBOR tags 4 and 5, which allows higher resolution or avoids rounding errors. Further keys can be registered in the Time Tag Map Keys registry.
sections.eli5: Think of a sticky note with one required line, the time, and optional extra lines. If you do not understand an optional line you can skip it, but if you do not understand a required line you must stop and say so.

sections.title: Sub-second Fractions
sections.content:
The keys -3, -6, -9, -12, -15 and -18 add an unsigned integer scaled by 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9, 1e-12, 1e-15 and 1e-18 respectively. An extended time MUST NOT contain more than one of them. The fraction is added to a base time in seconds given by key 1, which MUST also be present and MUST have an integer value.

These keys exist to make it easy to represent second plus decimal fraction pairs, as in C timespec. When loading such a value into a platform type, care is needed to meet its invariants, for example keeping the nanosecond part between 0 inclusive and 10^9 exclusive by adjusting the base time.
sections.eli5: The whole seconds go in one box, and the tiny leftover bit goes in another box labeled with how small the unit is.

sections.title: Timescales and Clock Quality
sections.content:
Keys -1, -13 and 13 give a timescale; key 13 is critical, and -1 and -13 have identical semantics. An extended time MUST NOT contain more than one of them. Value 0 is UTC with the POSIX epoch and value 1 is TAI with the PTP epoch (1 January 1970 00:00:00 TAI). If no key is present, 0 is implied. The RFC says there should be no "GPS" or "NTP" timescales, because those can be converted to TAI or UTC with a single addition or subtraction.

A group of keys describes the quality of the clock. Key -2 is ClockClass and key -4 is ClockAccuracy, both one-byte values taken from the PTP definitions, and key -5 is OffsetScaledLogVariance. Key -7 is Uncertainty and key -8 is Guarantee, each given as a number of seconds or as a duration. Uncertainty is the expanded uncertainty for k = 2 as defined in the GUM; Guarantee is the maximum deviation the source promises, as in RFC 3161.
sections.eli5: You can say which clock the time came from, and how far off that clock might be, a bit like writing "accurate to within a few thousandths of a second" next to a reading.

sections.title: Time Zone Hints and IXDTF Suffixes
sections.content:
Keys -10 and 10 carry a time zone hint as a text string in the time-zone-name or time-numoffset format of RFC 9557. Key -10 is an elective hint, while key 10 is critical and MUST be used when interpreting the entry. They MUST NOT both be present.

Keys -11 and 11 carry a map of IXDTF suffix keys and values, such as the calendar that best fits for showing the time to humans. Again 11 is critical, and when both are present their maps MUST NOT share map keys.

The RFC shows how the RFC 9557 example 1996-12-19T16:39:57-08:00[America/Los_Angeles][u-ca=hebrew] maps onto a time tag. It also notes that the numeric offset (-08:00) is lost when converting to POSIX time under key 1.
sections.eli5: You can attach a note saying which city's clock to show and which calendar to use, so people reading the time later see it the way the sender meant.

sections.title: Durations and Periods (Tags 1002 and 1003)
sections.content:
A duration is the length of an interval, given in SI seconds and possibly adjusted for conventional corrections of the chosen timescale. Tag 1002 is structurally identical to tag 1001, so all the same keys apply. It does not measure from an epoch but from the start to the end of an otherwise unspecified interval. The RFC notes that ISO 8601 durations are rather different and are not supported.

A period is a specific interval, tag 1003, holding an array. It is either a start and an end time, or a start or end time plus a duration. In the three-element form the missing start or end MUST be set to null and the third element is the duration. Exactly two of the three elements must be present and non-null.
sections.eli5: A duration is "it took two hours". A period is "from lunch until three o'clock", or "starting at lunch and lasting two hours".

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated tag 1001 (a map, extended time), tag 1002 (a map, duration) and tag 1003 (an array, period). IANA also updated the Data Item column for tag 1003 from map to array.

Two new registries were created. The Timescales registry requires both Expert Review and RFC Required, and starts with UTC as 0 and TAI as 1. The Time Tag Map Keys registry requires Specification Required. The designated expert is asked to give the shortest encodings to keys likely to see wide use, and to consider registering an elective key and a critical key as a negative and positive pair, as with -11 and 11.
sections.eli5: Official lists were opened for new clock types and new note types, so later documents can add their own without breaking old readers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8949 apply, and the new tags are not expected to raise more. Time itself still matters for security: ambiguities can be exploited where time is used for freshness or a validity span, and details such as the time zone or clock resolution can disclose characteristics of the emitting system.

Representations that allow complex and possibly inconsistent information are discussed in Section 7 of RFC 9557.
sections.eli5: Being unclear about time can be exploited, and extra details like your time zone can reveal things about your computer.
